default.p.test-17-p1.vietnamese:
In modern society, the trend of giving the highest priority to “efficiency” in every situation is growing stronger. Not only in the way we perform our work, but also in daily activities such as traveling and doing housework, as well as in hobbies and study, “time efficiency”—that is, how to achieve the greatest results in the least amount of time—is increasingly valued. Thanks to advances in information technology, we can instantly obtain the information we need and handle many tasks at once. Indeed, cutting out useless tasks to save time seems to offer great benefits to modern people living busy lives.

However, by trying to make every aspect of life more efficient, might we instead be losing something important? For example, when gaining a deep understanding of something or coming up with original ideas, periods of trial and error or taking a detour—things that may initially appear useless—are indispensable. Surely all of us have experienced unexpectedly finding a wonderful book while browsing the shelves of a bookstore without a specific purpose, or suddenly discovering a solution to a complicated problem while taking a purposeless walk. These “blank spaces” in time, deviating from a plan or purpose, are precisely what nurture human creativity and peace of mind.

Pursuing efficiency itself is not a bad thing. The real problem is that we fill the small amount of time created through greater efficiency with other tasks or plans, and consequently end up feeling as though something is constantly urging us on. In the first place, using time efficiently is merely a means of enriching our own lives. Therefore, should we not acknowledge not only the importance of managing time appropriately, but also the value of deliberately spending time without a purpose or having inefficient experiences, and develop the generosity to accept them?

(Note 1) Trial and error: Trying various methods, repeatedly failing, and gradually finding a better method.

(Note 2) Generosity: The quality of being broad-minded and able to accept other people, things, or situations.

default.p.test-18-p1.vietnamese:
When trying to concentrate on work or study, many people tend to seek an environment that is as quiet as possible. This is because silence is believed to be the ideal condition for improving performance, and removing more sound is thought to allow deeper immersion in the task. However, when there is no sound at all, some people may instead find small everyday sounds, such as the ticking of a clock’s second hand, irritating, or find that their own distracting thoughts keep surfacing and prevent them from concentrating.

Recent research in psychology and cognitive science has found that environments with a moderate level of ambient sound, such as the bustle of a café or the sound of rain, can promote creative thinking and concentration more effectively than a completely silent environment. In an overly quiet space, people’s awareness can unconsciously enter a state of tension, making their thinking less flexible. In contrast, moderate noise provides the brain with an appropriate level of stimulation, helping people remain relaxed while expanding their ideas.

Of course, not every kind of sound is beneficial. In an environment where the specific conversation at the next table can be heard clearly, the brain unconsciously tries to understand the meaning of the words, causing attention to be diverted. What is effective for maintaining concentration is being surrounded by a block of sound that has no particular meaning.

In short, what is truly necessary for concentrating on work is not completely blocking outside sounds, but skillfully accepting a moderate level of auditory stimulation suited to one’s condition and purpose. Absolute silence should not be regarded as the only ideal environment. Rather, skillfully adjusting the surrounding environment according to the task and one’s mood is the key to achieving high-quality results efficiently.

default.p.test-19-p1.vietnamese:
In modern society, using time efficiently, staying constantly focused on something, and producing results are highly valued. Whether at work or in study, people tend to believe that the ideal state is to minimize wasted time and always put their minds to use. For this reason, spending time leisurely and aimlessly without doing anything is often viewed negatively as “laziness” or “waste.” However, from the perspective of how the human brain functions, this “unfocused, relaxed time” plays a far more important role than we realize.

According to brain science research in recent years, the fact that people are not concentrating on a specific task does not mean that the brain has stopped working. On the contrary, researchers have discovered that there are neural networks that become actively engaged only when we release our conscious focus and relax. While these neural circuits are active, the brain organizes and rearranges past memories and the vast amount of accumulated information, unconsciously connecting them with one another. The solution that does not emerge even when we sit at a desk and rack our brains continuously, but suddenly flashes into our minds during an incidental moment such as taking a walk or bathing, is made possible by this mechanism.

Of course, this does not mean that good ideas will naturally appear if we simply relax and let our minds wander from the outset. As an essential prerequisite, it is indispensable to spend time thinking a problem through thoroughly. Only when there is sufficient “input” in the form of information gathering and thought can it be integrated and synthesized during periods of relaxed, unfocused time. Creative thinking becomes possible only when both elements—focused attention and letting go of conscious attention—come together.

If we fill our schedules all day in pursuit of efficiency and productivity and treat rest lightly, we will inadvertently lose the open space in which new ideas can emerge. To truly improve intellectual productivity, are we not also required to deliberately set aside time to pause conscious thought and free our minds, equivalent to the time we spend concentrating on our work?

((Note 1)) Laziness: Being idle and careless or messy.

default.p.test-20-p1.vietnamese:
In recent years, rapid advances in digital technology have brought revolutionary changes to our living environment. With a few actions on a smartphone, we can obtain the information we want in an instant, and find the shortest route to an unfamiliar destination in just a few seconds. In everyday life, “wasted time” and “inefficient work” have been thoroughly eliminated, and putting efficiency first has become an unquestioned moral standard in modern society. But can we really say that optimizing everything for efficiency will make our lives and minds truly richer?

For example, consider looking for a book we want to read. If we shop online, books suited to our tastes are automatically recommended on the screen based on our purchase history and past search trends, greatly reducing the effort required to search. By contrast, going all the way to a bookstore and browsing the shelves takes both time and effort, seeming inefficient and wasteful at first glance. Yet while wandering aimlessly among the bookshelves (Note 1), we may sometimes be drawn to specialized books in fields we normally have no interest in, or captivated by a book that happens to catch our eye. Such unexpected encounters with the unknown are precious experiences that we can never have in a world optimized solely for efficiency.

Furthermore, even when thinking deeply in order to understand the essence of something and develop our own ideas, a certain amount of “taking the long way around” and “trial and error” is essential. An answer found immediately through a search engine is convenient and fast, but it is difficult to retain in memory and often does not lead to deep understanding. By contrast, a conclusion that we struggle with and arrive at ourselves over time sinks into us (Note 2) and takes lasting shape within us. Precisely because we live in an age that values efficiency and speed above all else, shouldn't we dare to accept choices that require more effort and turn our attention to the hidden values found along indirect paths?

((Note 1)) Bookshelf: A shelf for books

((Note 2)) Become part of one's flesh and blood: Knowledge or experience sinks deeply into a person and becomes their own ability.

default.p.test-21-p1.vietnamese:
In modern society, with smartphones and the Internet becoming widespread, it has become taken for granted that we can immediately look up things we are curious about and receive answers on the spot. Knowledge that once required a deliberate trip to the library or asking someone else can now be obtained in the blink of an eye with a single touch of a fingertip. There is no doubt that this improved efficiency in accessing information has made our lives dramatically more convenient and greatly shortened the time needed to solve problems.

However, is an environment in which every question can receive an immediate answer, on the other hand, robbing us of the “time to think things through and ponder them deeply”? Precisely because answers can be found at once, we tend to skip the process of forming our own hypotheses or considering various possibilities in depth. When faced with something we do not understand, if we develop the habit of immediately relying on search tools, our ability to persevere and use our own minds to explore solutions to unfamiliar situations may decline.

Efficiently acquiring knowledge and thinking deeply may appear similar on the surface, but they are fundamentally different. Knowledge obtained instantly is easily forgotten as information used only for the moment, whereas understanding gained through repeated trial and error while holding on to a question becomes part of us and forms the foundation for long-term thinking ability. In other words, the time that seems “wasted”—when we patiently endure not having an immediate answer, choose not to look it up, and stop to think—is precisely the fertile soil that nurtures unique perspectives and profound insight.

Of course, I do not intend to deny the usefulness of quickly searching for information. In business and everyday life, efficient information gathering is indispensable in situations that require speed. However, rather than immediately searching for answers in every situation, it is important to occasionally maintain a deliberate distance from information and consciously make room in our lives to face unanswered questions, in order to sharpen our genuine thinking ability.

default.p.test-22-p1.vietnamese:
In modern society, the tendency to prioritize efficiency and speed above all else is steadily increasing. Thanks to the spread of the Internet, information we want to know can be searched for in just a few seconds, and in everyday life, reaching one’s destination by the “shortest distance” in every situation is often regarded as the wise way to live. The belief that it is rational not to waste time and to eliminate useless effort has permeated not only business but also fields such as education and personal hobbies.

However, is there anything we are gradually losing by optimizing everything for efficiency? For example, when learning something, if we simply receive the correct answer or a prepared summary, it may seem at first glance that we have acquired the knowledge in a short time. Yet without trying and failing on our own, without taking a “detour”—occasionally trying incorrect methods and experiencing failure—it is difficult to develop fundamental understanding and the ability to think deeply. It is precisely because we have time to struggle and make an effort ourselves that the knowledge we acquire becomes part of us and the ability to apply it is born.

Moreover, an attitude that relentlessly pursues efficiency also deprives us of opportunities for chance encounters and discoveries. If we focus only on heading straight toward our destination, we will be unable to notice the flowers blooming by the roadside along the way or unexpected scenery. Is it not precisely in winding detours or spare time that may seem unrelated to our purpose that hints for fresh ideas and a rich sense of humanity are often hidden?

Of course, I am not denying the importance of valuing efficiency in producing results within a limited amount of time. However, what matters is having the attitude to use the time created through efficiency optimization to carefully face what may initially seem “pointless,” rather than simply filling it with the next efficient task. True richness, one might say, does not lie in taking the shortest route, but in enjoying the detour while deepening one’s own thinking.

((Note 1)) Becoming part of oneself: Knowledge or ability becoming fully internalized and turning into one’s own practical ability.

In recent years, a lifestyle that values “efficiency”—trying to obtain as much information and as many results as possible in the shortest time by watching videos at double speed or reading summaries instead of entire books—has been spreading. In modern society, which changes rapidly and is overflowing with information, it is entirely understandable that people want to use their limited time efficiently, and situations that call for such quick thinking and resourcefulness certainly exist.

However, I cannot help questioning the practice of judging everything by efficiency alone. For example, when we take the time to read a book carefully, we are not simply stuffing knowledge into our heads. We pause to reflect on the author's words and formulate questions, or compare them with our past experiences in order to think more deeply and broadly. Sometimes, we may even let our thoughts wander toward matters not directly related to the plot or line of argument (Note 1). Is it not precisely these “apparently wasteful detours” that provide fertile ground for cultivating our own unique perspectives and deep insights?

The method of quickly absorbing only the key points is, in essence, merely the reception of easily understood conclusions that someone else has already arranged and summarized. In exchange for saving time, it carries the risk of eliminating the “process of struggling and thinking things through for oneself” (Note 2). No matter how convenient the technology or tools that appear, the time spent puzzling over things, trying, and making mistakes is indispensable for understanding their essence and deepening one's thinking.

Of course, I do not mean to reject optimization of efficiency altogether. For simple everyday tasks and administrative paperwork, cutting waste and completing them quickly is surely best. However, to build solid values of our own or generate creative ideas, is it not important to dare to spend time thinking things through at a leisurely pace rather than demanding an immediate answer?

((Note 1)) 思いを馳せる: To let one's thoughts wander to distant places or to the past or future.

((Note 2)) 削ぎ落とす: To trim away and remove unnecessary parts.

default.p.test-24-p1.vietnamese:
In modern society, thanks to the widespread use of the Internet and smartphones, we can easily obtain all kinds of information before taking any action. For example, even when traveling, it has become commonplace to research everything in advance in meticulous detail, including reviews of destinations, how crowded they are, and recommended routes, and then create a plan without any waste or risk of failure. In terms of enjoying things efficiently, gathering information beforehand is certainly convenient and seems useful.

However, if we place too much importance on knowing everything in advance and doing everything according to plan, might we not lose valuable opportunities such as unexpected discoveries and unplanned encounters? Sometimes, turning into a small alley we happen to notice along the way, or stopping at a restaurant that was not on the itinerary and chatting with its owner, is what creates unexpected emotions and deeply memorable experiences. If we are always afraid of failure and choose only safe, certain options, we will gradually become able to act only within the limits of our own imagination.

The same applies to solving problems in daily life and at work. When faced with unfamiliar problems, if we simply search for other people's successful examples or things that seem to be the correct answers and imitate them, we will never develop the ability to experiment, make mistakes, and think deeply on our own. The answers we arrive at after struggling with a problem using our own minds, sometimes taking roundabout paths and experiencing failure, are what lead to genuine understanding and creativity with an individual character. Today, we are being asked to reconsider our attitude of undervaluing the very processes of thinking and experience because we rely too heavily on convenience.

default.p.test-25-p1.vietnamese:
In modern society, the trend of valuing “efficiency” and “the shortest route” in everything is growing stronger. By using the search functions on smartphones and convenient apps, we can obtain not only the shortest route to a destination but also answers to questions we have within a few seconds. It could be said that we have entered an age in which avoiding wasted time and producing results as quickly as possible are highly valued in both work and daily life. As a result, it seems that we have become accustomed, without realizing it, to eliminating as much of the “process” as possible on the way to an answer or result.

Certainly, the improvement in convenience and productivity gained by eliminating waste is immeasurable. But does removing everything useless always produce good results for us? For example, when new ideas arise or we gain a deep understanding of the essence of something, “time spent wandering and getting lost” can instead play a decisive role. If we focus from the outset on finding only one correct answer and proceed straight toward it, we will miss unexpected discoveries and connections with other knowledge spread along the way.

It is through the process of struggling, repeatedly failing and experimenting, or branching off into information that initially seems unrelated to our purpose, that our thinking deepens and original insights are born. In other words, the seemingly inefficient and wasteful process of “getting lost” and “taking detours” is actually fertile ground (Note 1) for nurturing flexible, diverse ideas unconstrained by existing frameworks.

Of course, in urgent tasks and routine work, thoroughly pursuing efficiency is indispensable and beyond question. However, when making important decisions in life or engaging in creative activities, would it not ultimately lead to deeper fulfillment and greater creativity to do more than simply seek an obvious answer immediately, and instead have the peace of mind to calmly accept taking a detour?

(Note 1) Soil, land: Here, an environment that serves as the foundation for producing and nurturing something new.

default.p.test-26-p1.vietnamese:
In recent years, thanks to the spread of smartphones and the rapid advancement of AI technology, “wasted time” has been systematically eliminated from our everyday lives. Images and audio can be played at double speed, and an app can display the shortest route to a destination in an instant. Even when a question arises, we can simply enter words into a search engine and immediately receive an easy-to-understand summary answer. Many people probably believe that saving as much time as possible and reaching one's goal by the shortest route is the rational thing to do, and an essential ability for surviving in a rapidly changing modern society.

Certainly, improving efficiency in everyday work and simple operations is useful and directly connected to higher productivity. However, an attitude that always places efficiency first in everything has harmful effects that cannot be ignored. In the process of thinking that enables people to produce original ideas and deeply understand the essence of things, some degree of “getting lost or taking detours” is inherently indispensable. If we grow up being given the correct answer or shortest route from the outset, we will lose the valuable experience of trial and error—the process of posing questions ourselves and testing hypotheses.

It is through independently searching for answers while repeatedly experiencing failure that superficial knowledge becomes part of us and develops into practical, living wisdom. Even if efficiency shortens our working hours, a sense of mental spaciousness that allows deep insight cannot arise if we fill the extra time with other tasks. To nurture creativity and flexible judgment, it is essential to consciously secure “inefficient time” to leisurely reflect on things that may not be immediately useful, without stubbornly seeking efficiency.

Precisely because we live in a modern age that praises speed and immediate efficiency, should we not have the courage to stop without fearing uselessness or stagnation? Actions that appear useless at first glance, such as reading without a purpose or taking an aimless walk, conceal important seeds for making the next great leap in our thinking.
